title: Joining the dots
grammar: Discourse markers and cohesion (however, moreover, consequently, in contrast)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Great writing connects ideas. Learn discourse markers and make your argument flow from first line to last.
scene.intro: A pile of good points is not an argument. What turns a list into a line of thought is cohesion — the discourse markers that link one idea to the next. In this unit you read a feature article on a societal issue and learn how however, moreover, consequently and in contrast guide a reader from start to finish. You will plan the essay from Writing Part 1. For the Inspiring Nordic project, this is how you join the dots. Let's begin.

activities.title: Reading — a feature article on a societal issue

data.title: Joining the dots
data.author: mateo
data.text:
We live in the most connected age in history; paradoxically, many people have never felt more alone. This contradiction is the starting point of a feature article our Grade 11 club wrote together, and writing it taught us as much about structure as about the subject.

The topic was digital loneliness. Our first draft, Sofía admitted, was a heap of good points with no thread between them. Each sentence was true; nevertheless, the reader had no idea where the argument was going. However, the moment we added discourse markers, everything changed.

Consider the difference. “Social media connects us. It also isolates us.” Two flat statements. Now join them: “Social media undeniably connects us; however, it can quietly isolate us at the same time.” Moreover, once one idea flows into the next, the reader trusts the writer. Consequently, the argument feels not just true but inevitable.

Nadia made a sharp point: markers are not decoration. Used carelessly, a stray “therefore” promises a logic that isn't there. Liam agreed, adding that the best writers use these signposts sparingly, letting the ideas themselves do most of the work.

For the Inspiring Nordic project, our essays must read as a single, unbroken line of thought. A reader should never wonder how paragraph three relates to paragraph two. In contrast to a shopping list of opinions, a genuine argument moves — it builds, qualifies and concludes. Join the dots well, and the reader will follow you anywhere.

data.title: Discourse markers and cohesion
data.intro: Discourse markers are the signposts that link ideas across sentences and paragraphs. They tell the reader whether you are adding, contrasting, giving a result or concluding. Used well, they turn a list of points into an argument.

examples.text: The plan is cheap; however, it is risky.
It saves money; moreover, it saves time.
Cities grew fast; in contrast, villages emptied.

rules: Adding: moreover, furthermore, in addition. Contrast: however, nevertheless, in contrast.
Result: therefore, consequently, as a result. Concession: although, despite, even so.
Punctuation: after a full stop or semicolon, follow the marker with a comma — However, …; …; however, …

items.sentence: The idea was clever; ___, it was expensive.
She trained daily; ___, she won easily.
It saves money; ___, it protects the planet.
___ the rain, the match went ahead.
The north grew rich; ___, the south stayed poor.

data.script: Good morning, Grade 11. Part 1 of the Writing paper is always an essay, so today we focus on cohesion. A strong essay flows: each paragraph links to the next with markers like however, moreover and consequently. Plan first, then connect your ideas clearly. Mateo will share his essay outline first on Wednesday. Remember the structure: introduction, two main paragraphs, and a firm conclusion. Use a discourse marker to signal contrast, and another to add support. Bring your best linking words, and make your argument flow.

activities.title: Speaking — plan an essay. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, plan the two body paragraphs of an essay on a societal issue, connecting your points with discourse markers. Model: “Fast fashion is cheap; however, its true cost is paid by the planet. Moreover, it fuels waste.” 1) Which societal issue most deserves a full essay this year? 2) Can a well-linked argument make a weak idea sound convincing? 3) Which is harder: finding good points or joining them well? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write the two body paragraphs (10–12 sentences) of an essay on a societal issue for the Inspiring Nordic project, linking your ideas with at least four discourse markers (however, moreover, consequently, in contrast). Capital letters and full stops!
